body:
Festivals as living cultural heritage

Indian festivals reflect the relationship between communities, geographical conditions, agricultural activities, religious beliefs and historical traditions. Some festivals are celebrated across India under different regional names, while others are closely associated with a particular town, community or historical site.

For example, Uttarayan in Gujarat and Pongal in Tamil Nadu belong to the group of seasonal celebrations around Makar Sankranti. In contrast, Badamwari in Kashmir and Hampi Utsav in Karnataka have distinctive geographical and cultural associations.

A festival's association with a particular state does not necessarily mean that it is celebrated exclusively within that state. Such associations identify the regions where the festival has particular cultural significance.

Badamwari Spring Blossom Festival

Badamwari is associated with Srinagar in the Union Territory of Jammu and Kashmir. The name refers to an almond garden located in the old city of Srinagar, near the foothills of Koh-e-Maran, also known as Hari Parbat.

The flowering of almond trees announces the arrival of spring in the Kashmir Valley. The Badamwari Spring Blossom Festival celebrates this seasonal transformation and provides an opportunity to experience Kashmiri cultural traditions.

  • Location: Badamwari Garden, Srinagar.
  • Season: Early spring, generally March.
  • Natural association: Almond blossoms.
  • Cultural features: Traditional music, local food and community celebrations.

The precise flowering period depends on weather conditions. Therefore, the festival should be associated with early spring rather than an unchanging Gregorian calendar date.

Badamwari celebrates almond blossoms, not tulip blossoms. It belongs to the Kashmir Valley and should not be confused with festivals of Ladakh or Himachal Pradesh.

Hampi Utsav

Hampi Utsav, also known as Vijaya Utsav or Vijaya Utsava, is a cultural festival celebrated at Hampi in Karnataka. Hampi was the capital of the Vijayanagara Empire and is situated on the banks of the Tungabhadra River.

The festival celebrates the historical and cultural legacy of the Vijayanagara Empire. Music, dance, folk performances, processions and the illumination of historical monuments connect contemporary cultural activities with the heritage of the former imperial capital.

Unlike festivals determined by a fixed religious calendar, Hampi Utsav is organised on dates announced for individual editions. It has been held during different months, including November and February, generally during the cooler part of the year.

For example, Karnataka Tourism officially scheduled the 2026 edition for 13–15 February 2026. This was the announced schedule for that edition, not a permanent annual festival date.

Distinguishing the two festivals

Badamwari derives its significance primarily from a natural seasonal event, whereas Hampi Utsav derives its significance from historical and architectural heritage. Both contribute to regional tourism, but their central themes are different.

FeatureBadamwariHampi Utsav
RegionJammu and KashmirKarnataka
PlaceSrinagarHampi
Main associationAlmond blossomsVijayanagara heritage
SeasonEarly springVariable, generally cooler months

Prelims focus

  • Badamwari: Srinagar, Jammu and Kashmir.
  • Almond flowering marks the arrival of spring in Kashmir.
  • Hampi Utsav is also called Vijaya Utsav.
  • Hampi Utsav celebrates the heritage of the Vijayanagara Empire.
  • Hampi is situated along the Tungabhadra River.
  • Trap: Hampi Utsav does not have a permanently fixed Gregorian calendar date.

[References: NCERT, Exploring Society: India and Beyond, Class 6, Chapter 8, pp. 131–133; District Administration Srinagar, Government of Jammu and Kashmir, Badamwari; Ministry of Tourism, Utsav portal, Badamwari Spring Blossom Fest, 2022 event listing; Karnataka Tourism, Hampi destination guide and Hampi Utsava 2026: Dates, Events & Guide. Online sources consulted on 26 November 2026.]

title: Badamwari and Hampi Utsav: Regional Festivals and Their Cultural Significance

body:
Why several festivals occur in mid-January

Makar Sankranti marks the apparent movement of the Sun into the zodiac sign of Makara, or Capricorn, according to the traditional Indian solar calendar. It generally occurs on or around 14 January.

In many parts of India, this period is associated with agricultural prosperity, the gradual retreat of winter and seasonal harvesting. Different communities celebrate the occasion through local customs, food preparations, religious observances and agricultural traditions.

The regional festivals around Makar Sankranti illustrate unity in diversity: communities share a broad seasonal occasion but express it through different cultural practices.

Regional festivals around Makar Sankranti

Festival or regional namePrincipal state or regionDistinctive association
UttarayanGujaratKite flying and solar transition
LohriPunjab and HaryanaBonfires and winter festivities
MaghiPunjabObservance following Lohri
PongalTamil NaduHarvest thanksgiving and rice preparations
Magh Bihu or Bhogali BihuAssamHarvest completion and communal feasts
Pedda Panduga or SankrantiAndhra PradeshMajor seasonal harvest celebration
Makara SankramanaKarnatakaSolar transition and seasonal customs
Poush SankrantiWest BengalRice preparations and seasonal sweets
Khichdi ParvUttar PradeshKhichdi and religious observances
Shishur SaenkraatKashmirRegional winter Sankranti observance
Makar SankraatRajasthanSeasonal celebrations and kite flying
MakaravilakkuKeralaSabarimala pilgrimage observance

These observances occur around the same seasonal period, but they are not identical festivals. Lohri, for instance, is generally celebrated on 13 January, while Pongal extends over several days. Makaravilakku has a particularly important pilgrimage association rather than being simply another agricultural thanksgiving festival.

Uttarayan in Gujarat

Uttarayan is one of Gujarat's most distinctive seasonal festivals. It is celebrated through kite flying, particularly from rooftops, with Ahmedabad being a major centre of organised kite-flying festivities.

The term Uttarayan traditionally refers to the northward movement of the Sun. In Gujarati festival usage, it identifies the celebration of Makar Sankranti in mid-January.

Uttarayan and Makar Sankranti are closely associated in Gujarati tradition, but Makar Sankranti is not the astronomical winter solstice, which occurs in December.

Pongal in Tamil Nadu

Pongal is a harvest thanksgiving festival celebrated at the beginning of the Tamil month of Thai. Its central custom is the preparation of a rice dish, also called pongal, using newly harvested rice. Allowing the contents of the cooking pot to overflow symbolises abundance and prosperity.

The festival traditionally extends over 4 days, with different observances expressing gratitude for nature, agriculture, cattle and family life.

ObservanceCentral significance
BhogiRenewal and preparation for the festival
Thai Pongal or Surya PongalThanksgiving to the Sun
Mattu PongalHonouring cattle associated with agriculture
Kaanum PongalFamily gatherings and social visits

Lohri and Magh Bihu

Lohri is especially associated with Punjab and is also celebrated in Haryana and other parts of northern India. Families gather around bonfires and share seasonal foods such as sesame preparations, jaggery and rewri.

Magh Bihu in Assam marks the completion of an important agricultural harvest. It is also called Bhogali Bihu because food, abundance and communal feasting are central to the celebration.

Thus, the bonfire of Lohri, the rice preparation of Pongal and the kites of Uttarayan are distinctive cultural features of celebrations occurring within broadly the same seasonal period.

Prelims focus

  • Makar Sankranti is based on the traditional solar calendar.
  • Uttarayan: Gujarat; Pongal: Tamil Nadu.
  • Lohri: Punjab and Haryana, generally 13 January.
  • Magh Bihu and Bhogali Bihu are alternative names of the same Assamese festival.
  • Mattu Pongal honours cattle.
  • Trap: Makaravilakku and Onam are distinct observances in Kerala.

[References: NCERT, Exploring Society: India and Beyond, Class 6, Chapter 8, pp. 131–132, Figure 8.5; Gujarat State School Textbook Board, Social Science, Standard 7, English-medium 2021–22 edition, Chapter 8, pp. 42–44; Ministry of Tourism, Utsav portal, Harvest Festival, Lohri and Pongal sections; Incredible India, Pongal; Assam Tourism, Bihu Festival; Gujarat Tourism, International Kite Festival. Online sources consulted on 26 November 2026. The online Standard 7 textbook copy was consulted in place of the unreadable project Volume 09 scan.]

title: Makar Sankranti and the Mid-January Festivals of India

body:
Agricultural seasons and festival timing

A harvest festival celebrates agricultural production, the availability of new grain or the successful completion of a farming season. Some festivals also mark the beginning of cultivation or express hopes for a successful future harvest.

India has considerable regional variation in rainfall, temperature, crops and agricultural practices. Consequently, harvest festivals do not occur at the same time throughout the country.

  • Kharif crops are generally sown with the arrival of the monsoon and harvested during or after the rainy season. Paddy is an important example.
  • Rabi crops are generally sown during autumn or winter and harvested in spring. Wheat is an important example.

Regional cropping patterns can differ from these broad seasonal divisions. Festival timing must therefore be understood in relation to local agricultural conditions.

Major agricultural and harvest festivals

FestivalState or regionUsual periodAssociation
Vaisakhi or BaisakhiPunjab and HaryanaAprilWheat harvest
OnamKeralaAugust–SeptemberHarvest and Mahabali tradition
NuakhaiWestern OdishaAugust–SeptemberFirst consumption of new grain
Nabanna or NabanyaWest BengalNovember–DecemberNew rice harvest
WangalaMeghalayaGenerally NovemberGaro post-harvest thanksgiving
Chavang KutManipurNovemberCompletion of harvest
Tokhu EmongNagalandNovemberLotha Naga post-harvest festival
Puthari or HuthriKodagu, KarnatakaNovember–DecemberPaddy harvest

Vaisakhi: agricultural and religious significance

Vaisakhi is celebrated in April, usually on 13 or 14 April, and is closely associated with the harvesting of the wheat crop in Punjab. The festival also has particular religious importance for Sikhs because Guru Gobind Singh established the Khalsa in 1699 on the occasion of Vaisakhi.

Its agricultural and religious meanings coexist. Therefore, describing Vaisakhi exclusively as either a harvest festival or a religious festival would omit an important part of its significance.

Onam: the principal harvest festival of Kerala

Onam is celebrated in the Malayalam month of Chingam, generally falling in August or September. It is associated with the legendary homecoming of King Mahabali and with agricultural prosperity.

The main festive period traditionally extends over 10 days, beginning with Atham and culminating in the principal celebration of Thiruvonam.

  • Pookkalam: Decorative floral arrangements made on the ground.
  • Onasadya: A traditional festive meal, commonly served on a banana leaf.
  • Vallamkali: Traditional boat races associated with the festive season.

Onam must be distinguished from Vishu, Kerala's solar New Year observance in April. Both are associated with prosperity, but they occur in different seasons.

Nuakhai and Nabanna

Nuakhai is particularly important in western Odisha, including the Sambalpur region. Its name expresses the idea of eating newly harvested grain. The new produce is traditionally offered to the deity before being consumed by the community. The worship of Goddess Samaleswari is an important association in Sambalpur.

Nabanna is a Bengali celebration of newly harvested rice, particularly associated with the Bengali month of Agrahayan, corresponding approximately to November–December. Families prepare food from the new rice and express gratitude for the harvest.

Although both festivals celebrate new agricultural produce, their principal regions and usual seasonal periods are different.

The 3 Bihu festivals of Assam

Assam celebrates 3 principal Bihu festivals corresponding to different stages of the agricultural year.

Bohag Bihu or Rongali Bihu

Celebrated in mid-April, Bohag Bihu marks the Assamese New Year, the arrival of spring and the beginning of a new agricultural cycle. It is associated with music, dance and joyful community celebrations.

Kati Bihu or Kongali Bihu

Celebrated in mid-October, Kati Bihu occurs when crops are still developing in the fields. Food stocks may traditionally be limited during this period. Earthen lamps are lit and prayers are offered for the protection and successful growth of crops.

Magh Bihu or Bhogali Bihu

Celebrated in mid-January, Magh Bihu marks the conclusion of the harvest season. Community feasts and traditional bonfires express gratitude for agricultural abundance.

Rongali is associated with the beginning of cultivation, Kongali with the growing crop and Bhogali with the completion of harvest. These names refer to 3 distinct festivals, not interchangeable names for one festival.

Chapchar Kut: an agricultural festival before cultivation

Chapchar Kut is a major festival of Mizoram, generally celebrated in March. It is associated with the traditional cycle of jhum cultivation, a form of shifting cultivation.

The festival traditionally occurs after vegetation has been cleared from the cultivation site and while the cut vegetation is drying before the next stage of cultivation. It provides an interval of celebration before agricultural work resumes.

Chapchar Kut is therefore connected with agricultural preparation rather than the completion of a harvest. It should be distinguished from Chavang Kut of Manipur, which celebrates the end of harvesting.

Prelims focus

  • Vaisakhi: Punjab, April, wheat harvest and establishment of the Khalsa in 1699.
  • Onam: Kerala, Chingam, August–September.
  • Nuakhai: western Odisha; Nabanna: Bengal.
  • Wangala: Garo community of Meghalaya, post-harvest celebration.
  • Assam: Rongali in April, Kongali in October and Bhogali in January.
  • Trap: Chapchar Kut is associated with agricultural preparation, not completed harvesting.

[References: NCERT, Science, Class 8, 2018–19 edition, Chapter 1, Crop Production and Management, pp. 2 and 10–11; Assam Tourism, Bihu Festival; Kerala Tourism, Onam and Vishu festival descriptions; Incredible India, Vaisakhi Mela, Kut Festival and Tokhu Emong; Ministry of Tourism, Utsav portal, Nuakhai, 2024 event listing; Parampara Project, Nabanna; Meghalaya Tourism, Wangala Festival; District Administration Kodagu, Huthri Festival; Government of Mizoram, Chapchar Kut festival description. Online sources consulted on 26 November 2026.]

title: Harvest Festivals Across the Indian Agricultural Year
